people.name: Olof Hanson
body: Charles Thompson Memorial Hall in St. Paul was designed by a Deaf architect, Olof Hanson. MNopedia calls it the first social club in the United States designed exclusively for deaf people, and the Minnesota Council on Disability describes it as having "served as the nation's first Deaf club." The hall's own website goes further, calling it the first clubhouse for the deaf in the world.

Hanson was born in Fjälkinge, Sweden, on September 10, 1862, and came to the United States in 1875, at 13, settling with his mother, brother and sister on a farm near Willmar, Minnesota. He had lost hearing in one ear as a boy in Sweden and lost the rest soon after the family arrived. He graduated from the Minnesota School for the Deaf in Faribault in 1881, then from the National Deaf-Mute College in Washington, D.C., now Gallaudet University, in 1886. He received a master's degree from the college in 1889.

After a year studying architecture in Europe and a short spell in Philadelphia, he opened his own office in Faribault in 1896 and ran it until 1902, designing houses, stores, schools and churches. His designs included the North Dakota School for the Deaf at Devils Lake (1892) and a dormitory for Kendall School students on the Gallaudet campus (1895). In 1916 Margaret Brooks Thompson, widow of Charles Thompson, hired him to design the St. Paul hall in her husband's memory. It was dedicated that year and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.

From 1910 to 1913 Hanson was president of the National Association of the Deaf, a period when a federal Civil Service Commission rule barred Deaf people from taking government job exams. In 1899 he married Agatha Tiegel, then teaching at the Minnesota school. They moved to Seattle in 1902, where he practiced with partner Frank Thayer and later consulted for the University of Washington. He was ordained an Episcopal priest in 1929 and died in Seattle on September 8, 1933.
keyFacts: 1862: Born September 10 in Fjälkinge, Sweden; came to Minnesota in 1875.
1881: Graduated from the Minnesota School for the Deaf, Faribault.
1886: Graduated from the National Deaf-Mute College (now Gallaudet); master's degree 1889.
1896–1902: Ran his own architectural office in Faribault.
1910–1913: President of the National Association of the Deaf.
1916: Designed Charles Thompson Memorial Hall, St. Paul (National Register, 2011).
1933: Died September 8 in Seattle.
people.connectToWork: When your program chooses a meeting place, who decides whether it works for people who sign, and how early are they part of that decision?

people.name: Agatha Tiegel Hanson
body: In June 1893 a young Deaf woman gave the valedictory address at the National Deaf-Mute College in Washington, D.C. Her title was "The Intellect of Women." Agatha Tiegel argued that men and women were equally intelligent, a public case made decades before American women won the vote.

Tiegel was born in Pittsburgh on September 14, 1873, and became deaf, and blind in one eye, at age seven after spinal meningitis. The college, now Gallaudet University, had only recently begun admitting women. In 1892 she helped found a secret women's society, now the Phi Kappa Zeta sorority. Gallaudet's archives describe her as the first woman to earn a Bachelor of Arts from the college. The Gallaudet Library's biography guide notes that Alto May Lowman graduated the year before, so she is also described as its second woman graduate.

After graduating she taught for six years at the Minnesota School for the Deaf in Faribault. In 1899 she married the Deaf architect Olof Hanson. The couple later moved to Washington State and raised three daughters. She kept writing poetry throughout her life and died in Portland, Oregon, on October 17, 1959.
keyFacts: 1873: Born September 14 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
1893: Valedictorian at the National Deaf-Mute College (Gallaudet); delivered "The Intellect of Women."
1893–1899: Taught at the Minnesota School for the Deaf.
1899: Married architect Olof Hanson.
1959: Died October 17 in Portland, Oregon.
people.connectToWork: When a process asks about one part of someone's identity, such as language or disability, what might it miss about other barriers the person meets at the same time?

people.name: Cadwallader Lincoln Washburn
body: In 1904 a Deaf artist from one of Minnesota's best-known families went to Japan and Manchuria to cover the Russo-Japanese War for the Chicago Daily News, alongside his brother Stanley. Cadwallader Washburn later reported on the Mexican Revolution as well.

Washburn was born in Minneapolis in October 1866, the son of U.S. Senator William D. Washburn. He became Deaf at five after scarlet fever and spinal meningitis. He graduated from Gallaudet College in 1890, then studied architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, art at the Art Students League in New York and painting with William Merritt Chase, and later studied in Madrid and Paris.

In 1903 he took up etching. He exhibited at the Paris Salon and won a gold medal at the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco. Because etching strained his eyes, he later switched to painting, and he was a member of the National Academy of Design. He also published scientific papers on insects.

Gallaudet gave him an honorary Doctor of Science degree in 1924, and Bowdoin College an honorary doctorate in 1947. He died in Maine on December 21, 1965, at 99. Gallaudet's Washburn Arts Building is named for him.
keyFacts: 1866: Born in October in Minneapolis.
1890: Graduated from Gallaudet College; later studied architecture at MIT.
1903: Began etching.
Reported for the Chicago Daily News on the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) and the Mexican Revolution (1910–12).
1924: Honorary Doctor of Science, Gallaudet.
1965: Died December 21 in Maine, at 99.
people.connectToWork: If you assumed what work or schooling a Deaf person could do, what would that assumption rest on, and how could you ask instead?

people.name: Blanche Wilkins Williams
body: In the 1890s a young Black Deaf woman from the Minnesota school in Faribault wrote to Edward Miner Gallaudet, president of the only college for Deaf students in the country, asking what she needed to do to be admitted. Blanche Wilkins had graduated at the top of her class. Gallaudet College did not admit Black students, and would not until 1950.

Wilkins became deaf at an early age and enrolled at the Minnesota School for the Deaf when she was eight. She attended for ten years, and in 1893 she became the first Black woman to graduate from the school. She wrote to the college's president more than once and was turned away because of her race.

She went on to lead anyway. In 1895 she became the first Black Deaf woman to teach at the North Carolina school for Black Deaf students, by the Faribault Daily News account. She later taught in Texas and Illinois, settling in the Chicago area. In 1899, the year she married Charles Williams, she became the first Black Deaf person on the executive committee of the National Association of the Deaf, at a time when the association did not accept Black members. That rule lasted until 1965, and the association formally expressed regret in 2012. She died in Evanston, Illinois, on March 24, 1936.
In 2018 the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf named its newest residence hall Wilkins Hall, and in May 2023 Gallaudet awarded her a posthumous honorary Doctor of Humane Letters.
keyFacts: 1876: Born December 1.
1893: First Black woman to graduate from the Minnesota school, at the top of her class.
1899: First Black Deaf person on the National Association of the Deaf executive committee.
1936: Died March 24 in Evanston, Illinois.
2018: Wilkins Hall dedicated at the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf.
2023: Posthumous honorary doctorate from Gallaudet.
people.connectToWork: An access service can still exclude people by race. How would you find out whether the Deaf services you refer people to work for Deaf people of color?

people.name: Petra Fandrem Howard
body: In 1915 a young hard of hearing woman took charge of a new office in Minnesota state government. Petra Fandrem became chief of the state's newly established Labor Bureau for the Deaf, which Gallaudet's library guide calls the first of its kind in the country. She would spend more than forty years in vocational rehabilitation and employment services for Deaf people.

Howard was born in Minneapolis in 1891 and became hard of hearing at five. She attended public schools and the Minnesota School for the Deaf and graduated from Gallaudet College in 1912. Around 1913 she also campaigned for women's suffrage. A surviving photograph shows her carrying suffrage newspapers.

She married Jay Cooke Howard, a Deaf Duluth businessman who was president of the National Association of the Deaf from 1913 to 1917; they later divorced. From 1941 to 1946 she was the first woman president of the Minnesota Association of the Deaf. By the National Deaf Life Museum's account she retired in 1956 with a commendation from the governor. Gallaudet gave her an honorary doctorate in 1960 and inducted her into its Hall of Fame in 2014.
keyFacts: 1891: Born in Minneapolis; hard of hearing from age five.
1912: Graduated from Gallaudet College.
1915: Became chief of Minnesota's Labor Bureau for the Deaf.
1941–1946: First woman president of the Minnesota Association of the Deaf.
1960: Honorary doctorate, Gallaudet.
2014: Inducted into the Gallaudet University Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: Who leads or staffs the service you work with, and do people who are deaf, DeafBlind or hard of hearing hold decision-making jobs in it?

people.name: Roberta "Bobbi" Cordano
body: On October 9, 2015, Gallaudet University's board announced its next president, and the choice came from St. Paul. Bobbi Cordano, a Deaf lawyer and longtime Minnesota leader, became the first Deaf woman and the first openly LGBTQ person to lead the university. She took office on January 1, 2016, as its 11th president, and as of October 2026 Gallaudet's Office of the President still lists her in the role.

Born Deaf to parents who were both Gallaudet alumni, Cordano decided at 13 to become a lawyer after her sister faced discrimination. She graduated from Beloit College in 1986 with a sociology major and went on to law school at the University of Wisconsin–Madison.

She began her career as an assistant attorney general for the State of Minnesota. She later served as an assistant dean at the University of Minnesota's Hubert H. Humphrey Institute of Public Affairs and as vice president of programs at the Amherst H. Wilder Foundation in St. Paul, where she oversaw programs serving nearly 9,500 people. She is a founding member of Metro Deaf School and a founding board member of Minnesota North Star Academy, a charter high school for deaf and hard of hearing students.
keyFacts: 1986: Beloit College (sociology); law degree, University of Wisconsin–Madison.
Early career: Assistant attorney general, State of Minnesota.
Founding member of Metro Deaf School; founding board member of Minnesota North Star Academy.
Later: Vice president of programs, Amherst H. Wilder Foundation, St. Paul.
January 1, 2016: Became Gallaudet's 11th president; still listed as of October 2026.
people.connectToWork: When you look for an expert or a leader on a Deaf-related decision, whose experience and language are you counting as expertise?

people.name: Andrew Foster
body: In 1957 Andrew Foster arrived in Accra, Ghana, and opened the Accra Mission School for the Deaf, which BlackPast describes as the first school of its kind in Africa. Over the next 30 years this Black Deaf American would start dozens more, earning the title "Father of Deaf Education in Africa."

Foster was born on June 27, 1925, in the Ensley neighborhood of Birmingham, Alabama. In 1936, at 11, he and his younger brother became Deaf after spinal meningitis. He attended the Alabama School for the Colored Deaf, which offered no high school program, so at 17 he moved to Detroit. He finished high school by correspondence and in 1950 graduated from the Detroit Institute of Commerce. With a scholarship he entered Gallaudet College, and in 1954 he became the first African American to earn a bachelor's degree there. He added a master's in deaf education from Michigan State Normal College in 1955 and a second bachelor's in Christian missions from Seattle Pacific College in 1956.

In 1956 he founded the Christian Mission for Deaf Africans, now the Christian Mission for the Deaf. By BlackPast's count he founded 31 more schools for Deaf children in countries including Ivory Coast, Benin, Cameroon, Burkina Faso, Nigeria and Kenya, and set up training programs in others. He used both American and local sign languages in his teaching.
Foster died on December 3, 1987, in a plane crash in Rwanda while traveling to Kenya. Gallaudet had given him an honorary doctorate in 1970, and in 2004 it dedicated an auditorium in his name.
keyFacts: 1925: Born June 27 in Birmingham, Alabama; Deaf from 1936 after meningitis.
1954: First African American to earn a bachelor's degree from Gallaudet.
1956: Founded the Christian Mission for Deaf Africans.
1957: Opened the Accra Mission School for the Deaf in Ghana.
1970: Honorary doctorate from Gallaudet.
1987: Died December 3 in a plane crash in Rwanda.
people.connectToWork: A Deaf person who grew up in another country may have learned a different sign language, or schooling may have come late. How does your intake find that out without assuming?

people.name: Haben Girma
body: As a student at Lewis & Clark College, Haben Girma persuaded college officials to provide accommodations so that she could eat with other students in the cafeteria. A few years later she became the first DeafBlind person to graduate from Harvard Law School.

Girma was born on July 29, 1988, in Oakland, California. Her mother, Saba Gebreyesus, was a refugee who fled Eritrea in 1983 during its war of independence from Ethiopia; her father is Ethiopian. At 15 she traveled to Mali with the Oakland nonprofit buildOn to help build schools.

She graduated from Lewis & Clark in 2010 and from Harvard Law in 2013. That February President Obama named her a White House Champion of Change. She joined Disability Rights Advocates in Berkeley in 2013 and in 2014 represented a blind reader in a successful accessibility case against the digital library Scribd. In April 2016 she left to focus on advocacy outside the courtroom.
In August 2019 she published a memoir, Haben: The Deafblind Woman Who Conquered Harvard Law, which recounts childhood summers with her family in Asmara, Eritrea.
keyFacts: 1988: Born July 29 in Oakland, California.
2010: Bachelor's degree, Lewis & Clark College.
2013: First DeafBlind graduate of Harvard Law School; named a White House Champion of Change.
2013–2016: Attorney at Disability Rights Advocates.
2019: Published her memoir with Twelve.
people.connectToWork: Think of an ordinary part of your service, such as a waiting room or a shared meal. What would a DeafBlind person have to ask for to take part, and could you remove the need to ask?

people.name: Jelica Nuccio
body: In 2007, in Seattle, DeafBlind people began exploring their tactile instincts and building a way to communicate directly by touch, rather than through sighted interpreters. Out of that work grew Protactile, which a 2022 OPB report described as a new language born in the Northwest. Linguists Terra Edwards and Diane Brentari cite Jelica Nuccio and aj granda, both DeafBlind, as its leading educators and the authors of its "protactile principles."

In 2007 Nuccio became the first DeafBlind director of the DeafBlind Service Center in Seattle, where she began advocating for DeafBlind people to communicate with each other without interpreters. By the Lincoln Chronicle's account she did not set out to create a language. After 21 years in Seattle she moved to Monmouth, Oregon, in 2018. There she runs Tactile Communications and has been lead trainer for Western Oregon University's DeafBlind Interpreting Institute, which received a $2.1 million federal grant in 2021.

Visual sign languages happen in what researchers call air space, which DeafBlind people cannot see. Protactile is produced in contact space, on the body of the person being addressed. Listeners give continuous feedback by tapping a partner's arm or leg, much as a hearing person might say "mm-hmm."
keyFacts: 2007: Protactile begins among DeafBlind people in Seattle.
2007: First DeafBlind director of the DeafBlind Service Center, Seattle.
2018: Moved from Seattle to Monmouth, Oregon, where she runs Tactile Communications.
2021: Western Oregon University received a $2.1 million federal grant for DeafBlind interpreter training.
people.connectToWork: Does your access process assume a DeafBlind person uses ASL with an interpreter, or does it ask first how the person communicates, including by touch?

people.name: I. King Jordan
body: In March 1988 Gallaudet University's board chose a hearing woman as president, passing over two Deaf finalists. Students shut down the campus. Their protest, Deaf President Now, made national news for a week. It ended when the board reversed its choice and named I. King Jordan, dean of the College of Arts and Sciences, as Gallaudet's first Deaf president since its founding in 1864.

Jordan was born in Glen Riddle, Pennsylvania, to parents who worked in mills. After high school he served four years in the U.S. Navy. At 21 he was badly injured when a car hit him while he was riding his motorcycle, and he became profoundly Deaf. He earned a bachelor's degree in psychology at Gallaudet in 1970, then a master's (1971) and a doctorate (1973) at the University of Tennessee. He joined Gallaudet's faculty in 1973, chaired the psychology department from 1983, and became dean in 1986.

He served as president until December 31, 2006. In 1990 he was a lead witness before Congress for the Americans with Disabilities Act, and Presidents George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton each appointed him vice chair of the President's Committee on Employment of People with Disabilities. In 2001 he received the Presidential Citizens Medal.
keyFacts: Born in Glen Riddle, Pennsylvania.
At 21: Became Deaf after a motorcycle accident while serving in the Navy.
1970: Bachelor's degree, Gallaudet; master's (1971) and doctorate (1973), University of Tennessee.
March 1988: Named Gallaudet's first Deaf president after the Deaf President Now protest.
December 31, 2006: Stepped down as president.
people.connectToWork: In a decision about Deaf services, who sets the agenda, who controls the money, and who only gets asked for input after the plan exists?

people.name: William Ellsworth Hoy
body: In October 1961 a 99-year-old man stood at Crosley Field in Cincinnati, built on the site of his old home field, and threw the ceremonial first pitch before Game 3 of the World Series. William Ellsworth Hoy had played his first major league game more than 70 years earlier.

Hoy was born on May 23, 1862, in Houcktown, Ohio. Meningitis left him Deaf at three. He entered the Ohio School for the Deaf in 1872 and graduated in 1879 as valedictorian. He reached the major leagues in 1888 with Washington and led the National League in stolen bases as a rookie. He went on to play for Buffalo, St. Louis, Cincinnati, Louisville and the Chicago White Sox, finishing with 596 stolen bases and about 2,048 hits; SABR notes that totals vary from 2,044 to 2,054 by database.

In his day he was called "Dummy," a common label for Deaf people then and offensive today, so this page uses his name. He has long been credited with inspiring umpires' hand signals. SABR reports that historians dispute this, so treat it as a popular story and not a fact.
Hoy died in Cincinnati on December 15, 1961. Gallaudet University dedicated its baseball field as Hoy Field on April 8, 2001, and he entered the Cincinnati Reds Hall of Fame in 2003.
keyFacts: 1862: Born May 23 in Houcktown, Ohio; Deaf from age three.
1879: Graduated from the Ohio School for the Deaf.
1888: Major league debut; led the National League in stolen bases.
Last major league season 1902, with one more minor league season in 1903.
1961: First pitch before Game 3 of the World Series; died December 15.
2001: Gallaudet's baseball field named for him; 2003: Cincinnati Reds Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: Which words in your forms, files or everyday speech came from an earlier time, and who could you ask about what they mean to people now?

people.name: Laura Redden Searing
body: During the Civil War, the St. Louis Republican sent a young Deaf woman to Washington, D.C., to report on politics and the military. Laura Redden interviewed President Abraham Lincoln, who also bought her books. Her readers knew her as "Howard Glyndon," a male pen name. By the National Deaf Life Museum's account she chose it because a man's name drew more attention, though her own name appeared beside it.

Laura Catherine Redden was born on February 9, 1839, in Somerset County, Maryland, by the State Historical Society of Missouri's account, which notes that some sources give 1840. Her family moved to St. Louis when she was a child, and spinal meningitis left her Deaf at about 11. She enrolled at the Missouri school for the deaf in Fulton in 1855. In 1858 she became editor of the St. Louis Presbyterian and began publishing in the Missouri Republican.

In 1862 she published Notable Men, biographies of members of Congress. Her 1864 collection Idylls of Battle and Poems of the Rebellion brought national attention. From 1865 to 1868 she studied languages in Europe and wrote for the New York Times and other papers. Back in New York she wrote for the Evening Mail and for magazines such as Harper's. From 1870 she studied speech and lipreading, including a year under Alexander Graham Bell, and in her articles urged that deaf schools teach speech along with sign language.

In 1872 she signed a petition supporting women's voting rights, and in 1875 she published a suffrage column in the Evening Mail. She married Edward Whelan Searing in 1876, had a daughter in 1880, moved to Santa Cruz, California, in 1886, and divorced in 1889. She died in 1923.
keyFacts: 1839: Born February 9 in Somerset County, Maryland; Deaf at about 11.
Civil War: Washington correspondent for the St. Louis Republican as Howard Glyndon; interviewed Lincoln.
1862: Notable Men. 1864: Idylls of Battle and Poems of the Rebellion. 1873: Sounds from Secret Chambers.
1865–1868: Correspondent in Europe.
1872 and 1875: Signed a suffrage petition; wrote a suffrage column.
1923: Died.
people.connectToWork: Deaf people have long disagreed about speech and sign. How does your process let a person choose their own communication without treating one choice as the right one?

people.name: Marlee Matlin
body: At the 59th Academy Awards in 1987, Marlee Matlin won Best Actress for Children of a Lesser God. She was 21, and by the Jewish Women's Archive's account she remains the youngest woman to win that award.

Matlin was born on August 24, 1965, and grew up in Morton Grove, a suburb of Chicago. She lost her hearing at 18 months. At seven she began attending the Center on Deafness and the Arts in Chicago, and in the summer of 1972 she played Dorothy in its production of The Wizard of Oz, using both speech and sign.

She earned four Emmy nominations, all for guest roles: Seinfeld and Picket Fences (1994), The Practice (2000) and Law & Order: Special Victims Unit (2004). She had featured roles on The West Wing, The L Word and Switched at Birth.

She has long championed closed captioning. In 1987 she became a spokesperson for the National Captioning Institute, and in 1990 she appealed to Congress for captioned television, supporting the Television Decoder Circuitry Act. She wrote the children's book Deaf Child Crossing (2002) and the memoir I'll Scream Later (2009). In 2021 she starred in CODA, about a hearing daughter in a Deaf family, with Deaf actors playing the Deaf characters; its cast won the Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding cast.
keyFacts: 1965: Born August 24; Deaf from 18 months.
1987: Academy Award for Best Actress, Children of a Lesser God.
1987: National Captioning Institute spokesperson; 1990: supported the Television Decoder Circuitry Act.
Four Emmy nominations for guest roles (1994, 1994, 2000, 2004).
2021: CODA; its cast won the SAG Award for outstanding cast performance.

people.name: Robert H. Weitbrecht
body: In 1964 two Deaf men connected their teletypewriters over an ordinary telephone line and typed to each other across a long distance. The device that made it possible was an acoustic coupler built by Deaf physicist Robert Weitbrecht.

Weitbrecht was born deaf on April 11, 1920, in Orange, California. He was a lifelong amateur radio operator. He earned a bachelor's degree in astronomy from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1942 and later a master's from the University of Chicago. He worked at the University of California Radiation Laboratory, the U.S. Naval Air Missile Test Center and Yerkes Observatory, and from 1957 at the Stanford Research Institute.

In 1964 James C. Marsters, a Deaf orthodontist in Pasadena, approached him about getting teletypewriters to work over phone lines. Weitbrecht designed a coupler, an early form of modem, that turned a machine's electrical signals into tones a phone handset could carry. The first successful transmission ran between Weitbrecht's home in Redwood City and Marsters's in Pasadena. The partners reconditioned discarded Teletype machines and, with Deaf businessman Andrew Saks, formed Applied Communications, which marketed the coupler as the Phonetype.

The TTY became a standard way for Deaf people to place calls and led to relay services. Weitbrecht received the Laurent Clerc Award and, in 1974, an honorary doctorate from Gallaudet College. He died in May 1983 after being struck by a car while walking his dog.
keyFacts: 1920: Born April 11 in Orange, California.
1942: Astronomy degree, UC Berkeley; later a master's, University of Chicago.
1964: First long-distance TTY calls using his coupler, developed with James C. Marsters.
1974: Honorary doctorate, Gallaudet College.
1983: Died in May after being struck by a car.

people.name: Robert J. Smithdas
body: In 1953 Robert Smithdas earned a master's degree from New York University. The American Council of the Blind and Gallaudet's library guide call him the first DeafBlind person to earn one, and he spent the next half century opening paths to education and work for other DeafBlind people.

Smithdas was born on June 7, 1925, in Brentwood, Pennsylvania. Cerebrospinal meningitis took his sight and nearly all his hearing at four and a half. He attended the Western Pennsylvania School for Blind Children and Perkins School for the Blind, graduating in 1945, and graduated cum laude from St. John's University in Brooklyn in 1950. He communicated by the manual alphabet and braille and could use the Tadoma method, reading speech with his fingers on a speaker's lips and throat.

In 1950 he began working at the Industrial Home for the Blind in New York, now Helen Keller Services, and from 1960 to 1969 he was associate director of its Services for the Deaf-Blind. His advocacy helped win a federally funded demonstration program, and with Helen Keller and Peter Salmon he helped shape the 1967 amendments to the Vocational Rehabilitation Act that authorized the Helen Keller National Center, which he co-founded and where he directed community education.

He published the autobiography Life at My Fingertips and the poetry collections City of the Heart (1966) and Shared Beauty (1983), and was named Poet of the Year for 1960–61. His wife, Michelle, was also DeafBlind. He died in Fort Collins, Colorado, on July 17, 2014, at 89, and entered the American Printing House for the Blind Hall of Fame in 2017.
keyFacts: 1925: Born June 7 in Brentwood, Pennsylvania; DeafBlind from age four and a half.
1950: Bachelor's degree cum laude, St. John's University.
1953: Master's degree, New York University.
Co-founder of the Helen Keller National Center.
Poet of the Year 1960–61; autobiography Life at My Fingertips.
2014: Died July 17 at 89.

people.name: Claudia L. Gordon
body: Claudia Gordon was born in Jamaica. By her own account to the Jamaica Observer, when she suddenly lost her hearing at eight she was taken out of school and kept at home to do chores, and her mother succeeded in bringing her to the United States by the time she was 11. In New York she attended the Lexington School for the Deaf, where she learned sign language. She describes her experience as an immigrant at the intersections of race, disability and gender as the foundation of her work.

She graduated cum laude from Howard University and cum laude from American University's Washington College of Law, its first deaf graduate. In 2000 she received a Skadden Fellowship to work at the National Association of the Deaf Law Center. At the Department of Homeland Security's Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties she was the primary author of a 2004 executive order on people with disabilities in emergency preparedness, and she received the Secretary's Gold Medal in 2006 for her work around Hurricane Katrina.

In the Obama administration she was chief of staff of the Labor Department's Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs and associate director of the White House Office of Public Engagement. She later worked as a senior accessibility strategist at Sprint and T-Mobile. She took her oath as a member of the National Council on Disability in November 2022 and became its Chair in April 2024. As of October 2026 the council's member page names Neil Romano as acting chairman and does not list Gordon.
keyFacts: Born in Jamaica; Deaf at eight; in the United States by 11.
First deaf graduate of American University's Washington College of Law.
2000: Skadden Fellow, National Association of the Deaf Law Center.
April 2024: Chair of the National Council on Disability; not listed on its member page as of October 2026.

people.name: Talila "TL" Lewis
body: Berkeley Law describes Talila A. Lewis as a Black, queer, nonbinary disabled abolitionist, community lawyer, educator and artist who communicates in signed, written, spoken and felt language. Lewis built the only national database of deaf, blind and disabled people in U.S. prisons.

In 2011 Lewis founded HEARD, originally Helping Educate to Advance the Rights of Deaf Communities, which by 2014 had become a cross-disability abolitionist nonprofit. Lewis served as its volunteer director for more than a decade before handing leadership to others in December 2023. Lewis earned a law degree from American University Washington College of Law in 2014, taught at Rochester Institute of Technology's National Technical Institute for the Deaf from 2014 to 2017, and was named a White House Champion of Change in 2015.

HEARD's campaigns worked to free deaf and disabled elders and wrongfully convicted people. Lewis also wrote a widely cited "living definition" of ableism. Lewis's own site avoids pronouns and repeats the name, so this page does too.
keyFacts: 2011: Founded HEARD; volunteer director until December 2023.
2014: Law degree, American University Washington College of Law.
2015: White House Champion of Change.
Built a national database of deaf, blind and disabled people in prisons.

institutions.name: Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf
aliases: Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf (MSAD)
institutions.type: State residential and day school for Deaf and hard of hearing students
body: In 1858 Minnesota's first state legislature agreed to place a school for Deaf children in Faribault if local citizens donated 40 acres. They did, but nothing more happened for five years. In September 1863 the first Deaf students, eight that first year, moved into a rented store building in Faribault, with Roswell H. Kinney of the Ohio School for the Deaf as first superintendent. Blind students were also admitted until a separate department opened in 1866. Long known as the Minnesota School for the Deaf, it is now the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf.

By the school's own account to MPR News, signing has always been permitted there, even in the decades when many schools insisted on speech and lipreading, and it now teaches in a bilingual ASL and English approach. Its graduates include architect Olof Hanson (1881), labor advocate Petra Fandrem Howard, and Blanche Wilkins Williams, the first Black woman to graduate, in 1893. Its street address is Olof Hanson Drive, and its residence hall named in 2018 is Wilkins Hall.

The campus has two buildings listed on the National Register of Historic Places: the Administration and Girl's Dormitory and Noyes Hall (listed in 1975). The school offers family ASL classes and is part of the Minnesota State Academies, which also includes the Minnesota State Academy for the Blind and an online academy. In 1993 students called for the school to hire a Deaf administrator.
keyFacts: 1858: Legislature agreed to place the school in Faribault.
1863: Opened in September with eight students.
1975: Noyes Hall listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
2018: Wilkins Hall named for Blanche Wilkins Williams.
Address: 615 Olof Hanson Drive, Faribault.
institutions.connectToWork: When a person mentions the school they went to, what might you ask to learn what it means to them, instead of treating it as one line of education history?

institutions.name: National Association of the Deaf
institutions.type: National civil rights organization founded by Deaf people
body: On August 25, 1880, Deaf leaders meeting in Cincinnati founded the National Association of the Deaf. Its first president was Robert P. McGregor; Edmund Booth of Iowa chaired the first convention. It was incorporated in Washington, D.C., in 1900, opened its first home office in Chicago in 1950, and has been based in Silver Spring, Maryland, since the early 1970s.

Minnesota's Olof Hanson was its president from 1910 to 1913, when a federal rule barred Deaf people from civil service exams. It worked for the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990. In 2015 it sued Harvard and MIT over uncaptioned online content; Harvard agreed in late 2019 and MIT in February 2020 to caption what they post. It describes its mission as preserving, protecting and promoting the civil, human and linguistic rights of deaf and hard of hearing people, and says its use of Deaf includes DeafBlind, DeafDisabled, hard of hearing and late-deafened people. As of its September 2026 news, it was back in court defending an order requiring ASL interpreters at White House briefings.

Its history also includes exclusion. It did not accept Black members until 1965, a rule for which it formally expressed regret in 2012, and Black Deaf people built their own organizations, including National Black Deaf Advocates.
keyFacts: 1880: Founded August 25 in Cincinnati.
1910–1913: Olof Hanson of Minnesota served as president.
1965: Black members first accepted; 2012: formal statement of regret.
2019–2020: Captioning settlements with Harvard and MIT.

institutions.name: Deaf West Theatre
body: In 2003 a Broadway revival of the musical Big River opened with Deaf and hearing actors sharing the stage, signing in American Sign Language while other performers voiced the lines in English. The production came from Deaf West Theatre, and it earned a Tony nomination for Best Revival of a Musical in 2004 and a Tony Honor for Excellence in Theatre.

Deaf West was founded in 1991 by Ed Waterstreet, a Deaf actor shaped by his years at the National Theatre of the Deaf, and his wife, Linda Bove, known for her long-running role on Sesame Street. Its productions are performed in ASL with simultaneous spoken English, so Deaf and hearing audiences watch the same show together. Waterstreet retired as artistic director in 2012 and is president emeritus of its board.
Its 2015 Broadway revival of Spring Awakening, which began in a 99-seat Los Angeles theater, received three 2016 Tony nominations. DJ Kurs, artistic director since 2012, guided it to Broadway.
keyFacts: 1991: Founded in Los Angeles by Ed Waterstreet and Linda Bove.
2003: Big River on Broadway; 2004 Tony nomination and a Tony Honor.
2015: Spring Awakening on Broadway; three Tony nominations in 2016.
Performs in ASL with simultaneous spoken English.
institutions.connectToWork: In your next public event, would a Deaf participant and a hearing participant experience the same thing at the same time? What would you change so they could?

institutions.name: Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing
aliases: Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing
body: The Minnesota Legislature created this body in 1985; its statute's history begins with that year's first special session. By the Legislative Reference Library's account it began as the Hearing Impaired Council, became the Minnesota Commission Serving Deaf and Hard of Hearing People in 1993, and was renamed again in 2008 on the way to its current name. State law names it the state's principal agency to advocate for equal access for these Minnesotans.

It advises the governor, the legislature, the courts and state agencies, including DHS, and helps individuals and parents advocate for themselves. By statute it has ten members appointed at large and one from each of up to five advisory committees. At least half of the voting members must be deaf, DeafBlind or hard of hearing, and at least one must be a parent or guardian of a person who is. The director of the DHS division is an ex officio, nonvoting member. It also hosts the Minnesota Collaborative Plan for education and sends email bulletins with ASL video.
keyFacts: 1985: Created by the Minnesota Legislature.
At least 50 percent of voting members must be deaf, DeafBlind or hard of hearing.
Website: mn.gov/deaf-commission.
institutions.connectToWork: Before a policy that affects these Minnesotans moves forward, at what point do you bring in the Commission, and what can it still change by then?

institutions.name: DHS Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services Division
aliases: Deaf and Hard of Hearing Services Division
DHS Deaf and Hard of Hearing Services Division
institutions.location: St. Paul, with regional services statewide
body: This Department of Human Services division serves, advocates for, and gives information and training about Minnesotans who are deaf, DeafBlind or hard of hearing. By law it maintains a statewide network of regional culturally and linguistically affirmative services. It also provides culturally and linguistically affirmative mental health services for people who use a visual language such as ASL, and it assesses the supply of interpreters and captioning and keeps a statewide list of providers.

Its governing law, section 256C.233, dates from 1996 and was most recently amended in 2024, and the Legislature created the Deaf and Hard of Hearing Services Act (sections 256C.21 to 256C.26) and the division itself in 1980. Grants through the division cover identified areas of need such as DeafBlind services, family services, interpreting and mental health.
keyFacts: Section 256C.233 dates from 1996; most recently amended in 2024.
Named grant areas include DeafBlind, family, interpreting and mental health services.

disability.intro:
This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here the page means people who are Deaf, DeafBlind, hard of hearing, late-deafened or DeafDisabled, who differ in language, in when and how they became deaf, in race, faith and immigration history, and in whether they have other disabilities. ASL and Deaf engagement are language access and cultural relations at once, and nobody should be asked to choose. No Minnesota study of how these Minnesotans or their families understand disability was found, and nothing on traditional healing among them.

Faith life is documented: Bread of Life Deaf Lutheran in Minneapolis (founded 1956) worships in ASL; the Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis has a deaf ministry at Our Lady of Mount Carmel, where about 50 of 170 members were deaf or hard of hearing in 2019; and the Minnesota Deaf Muslim Community held a Deaf Iftar with Tarawih prayer in 2024.

The research cited here on Deaf immigrants comes from Finland. Several points rest on publishers' descriptions and news features, not the books themselves.
questions: What language and communication works best for you: ASL, Protactile, another sign language, captioning, spoken English, writing, or something else?
Which words do you use for yourself: Deaf, DeafBlind, hard of hearing, DeafDisabled, a person with a disability, or something else?
Has anyone given you a label or a diagnosis about your hearing, vision or anything else? Who gave it to you, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Is there an interpreter or a kind of interpreter who works well for you, or one you would rather not use?
For touch or low-vision communication, what do you need from us with lighting, seating, support people and extra time?
Who do you want in this conversation, and who do you not want speaking or interpreting for you?
Did you grow up using a different sign language, or learn sign language later in life? What should we know so we can communicate well with you?
If you would like to tell me, how did your deafness or hearing or vision change come about, and does that history matter for what you need today?
Have past experiences with schools, doctors, police or courts affected how you feel about using services? What would make this safer?

context.heading: Language, culture and disability
body: Carol Padden and Tom Humphries, in Deaf in America, use capital-D Deaf for people who share a natural language and a culture, and describe a tension between how Deaf people see themselves and how the hearing world has seen them, including schools that forbade signed language. The 2014 collection Deaf Gain, edited by H-Dirksen L. Bauman and Joseph J. Murray, asks what deafness adds to the wider community. These points rest on the publishers' descriptions. They are a starting point and describe no individual.

Minnesota law holds both views at once. It requires services that are culturally and linguistically affirmative, and those services sit inside the Department of Human Services. Some people reject the word disability and others use it, for example when claiming legal rights or when they have other disabilities. Let each person say which words fit, and do not make access depend on the answer.

sources.label: Harvard University Press, Deaf in America
University of Minnesota Press, Deaf Gain (2014)
Minnesota Statutes § 256C.233

context.heading: DeafBlind experience and Protactile
body: DeafBlind experience is not Deaf experience with vision removed. Edwards and Brentari (2021) studied Protactile in groups of DeafBlind people in the United States who, for the most part, were born sighted, learned ASL as children and became blind slowly over decades. Before the protactile movement, the authors write, the response to that change was growing dependence on sighted interpreters. Protactile is signed on the body and uses touch feedback such as taps. It is one study of one group, and many DeafBlind people communicate in other ways, including braille and tactile signing.

The Christian Science Monitor (2020) reported that Protactile began in Seattle in 2007 among DeafBlind people who wanted to communicate directly. Do not route decisions through a sighted or hearing family member or support person by default.

sources.label: Edwards and Brentari, Frontiers in Psychology (2021)
Christian Science Monitor, In one revolutionary language, a community taps the power of touch (2020)

context.heading: Hard of hearing and late-deafened experience
body: Hard of hearing people may not sign or see themselves as part of Deaf culture, and some do. The National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders reports that about 15 percent of American adults, 37.5 million people aged 18 and over, report some trouble hearing. That is self-report and a national count, it includes mild difficulty, and it says nothing about identity or language. Minnesota figures with denominators exist: the State Demographic Center (Feb. 2026, 2023 American Community Survey one-year data) counts about 203,500 Minnesotans with a hearing disability, meaning deaf or serious difficulty hearing, within a state disability total of about 667,700 (11.5 percent of the population), and about 132,000 of them are 65 or older. Minnesota Compass (July 2026, 2024 American Community Survey) reports that 13 percent of Minnesotans 65 and older have hearing limitations. These are self-reported and do not identify who signs.

Ask about captioning, assistive listening and written follow-up rather than assuming ASL. Groups such as the Twin Cities chapter of the Hearing Loss Association of America are organized around this experience.

sources.label: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, Quick Statistics About Hearing
Hearing Loss Association of America, Twin Cities Chapter

context.heading: Family and decision-making
body: More than 90 percent of deaf children in the United States are born to hearing parents, according to Mitchell and Karchmer (2004), as cited by the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders. That national figure on students is about parents' hearing and tells you nothing about whether a family shares a language. Ask who communicates with whom, and how.

Speak to the person directly, not to the interpreter or family, and do not use family members, especially children, as interpreters. Minnesota law requires at least one parent or guardian on the state Commission, and at least half of its voting members must themselves be deaf, DeafBlind or hard of hearing.

sources.label: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, Quick Statistics About Hearing
Minnesota Statutes § 256C.28

context.heading: Black ASL and interpreter match
body: Carolyn McCaskill and colleagues described Black ASL in The Hidden Treasure of Black ASL (Gallaudet University Press, 2011), tracing it to segregated Southern schools for Black deaf students. McCaskill told The Washington Post in 2012 that when she arrived at a newly integrated Alabama school in 1968 she could not understand her white teacher's signing. A signer may not be understood by an interpreter trained only in mainstream ASL, and the reverse is also true. Ask, and do not assume from how anyone looks.

The Registry of Interpreters for the Deaf offers two national certifications: the National Interpreter Certification, held by hearing interpreters, and the Certified Deaf Interpreter certification. Ask whether a Deaf interpreter working with a hearing interpreter would help, especially where someone uses another country's sign language or has had limited formal language.

sources.label: Gallaudet University Press, The Hidden Treasure of Black ASL
Atlanta Black Star, The Hidden Treasure of Black Signs (2017)
Registry of Interpreters for the Deaf, Available Certifications

context.heading: Deaf immigrants and refugees
body: The one study found is an ethnography of deaf asylum seekers in Finland (Sivunen, 2019). It reports language barriers "from day one", that sign language classes improved participants' well-being, and that Deaf volunteers were central to helping them take part in society. Some participants had another country's sign language, and some had used no formal sign language before. It is a small study in another country. No U.S. or Minnesota study of this was found. Minnesota evidence does exist: 11 percent of students with a deaf or hard of hearing primary label in 2024-25 also receive English learner services, and 12 percent are Hispanic or Latino and 11 percent Asian (Minnesota Department of Education, 2026). The Commission's 2025-2030 Collaborative Plan, prepared with Wilder Research, records professionals saying Somali, Hmong and Spanish-speaking families face added barriers, and the Minnesota Deaf Muslim Community is an organized group serving Deaf Muslims. Culture-specific sources for these communities' Deaf residents are still missing.

sources.label: Sivunen, Societies 9(1) (2019)

context.heading: Justice systems and trust
body: HEARD documents that deaf and disabled people in prisons and jails often lack communication access, and supports them in getting legal and emotional support in their own language. This is advocacy documentation and not a Minnesota count. Check what communication access a person actually had before relying on a police, court or prison record.

communityRoutes.purpose: Three Lutheran Social Service of Minnesota programs for families with a deaf or hard of hearing child. In the Deaf Mentor Family Program, trained Deaf mentors teach ASL and other communication techniques and introduce Deaf community, at home or another place the family chooses; it focuses on younger children and is available to any deaf or hard of hearing child from birth to 21. Snapshots is for families whose child is newly identified. EMPOWER is eight self-advocacy sessions for youth ages 7 to 21.

organizations.intro: Deaf, DeafBlind and hard of hearing Minnesotans live statewide, and organize through Deaf-led and DeafBlind-led groups, schools, family programs, congregations and peer groups for people with acquired hearing loss. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts or which group speaks for them.
